title: Insurance Sales Agencies: Structure, Management, and Best Practices

questions.stem: In a pyramid retail agency structure, the primary financial incentive for a Unit Manager to actively develop the productivity of agents on their team is:

opts.x: A fixed monthly salary paid regardless of team performance.
An overrider commission calculated as a percentage of the production generated by the agents they supervise.
A share of the renewal commission from policies sold before the agents joined the unit manager's team.
A government-mandated supervisory allowance set by NAICOM.

questions.answer: (B) An overrider commission calculated as a percentage of the production generated by the agents they supervise.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

The overrider (also called override commission) is the financial mechanism that aligns the Unit Manager's personal income with the productivity of their team. The Unit Manager earns a percentage (typically 5–10%) of all first-year and renewal commission generated by every agent they supervise. This means the Unit Manager's income grows directly as their agents' productivity grows — creating a powerful incentive to recruit, train, develop, and retain productive agents. It is the commercial engine of the pyramid agency model.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) A fixed salary independent of team performance would remove the productivity incentive entirely — the Unit Manager could earn the same by managing a poor team as by managing an excellent one. This is inconsistent with the pyramid model's incentive architecture.
(C) The renewal commission from pre-team policies belongs to the original selling agent (or the insurer if the agent has left) — not to a new Unit Manager who had no role in the original sale.
(D) There is no NAICOM-mandated supervisory allowance. Agency compensation structures are commercial arrangements between the insurer and its agency force.

questions.stem: The 13-month persistency rate for a retail agent is calculated as:

opts.x: The number of new policies submitted by the agent in the most recent 13 months.
The total commission earned by the agent in the past 13 months as a percentage of their target.
The proportion of policies issued by the agent 13 months ago that are still in force today.
The agent's policy submission rate expressed as a percentage of their appointment rate over 13 months.

questions.answer: (C) The proportion of policies issued by the agent 13 months ago that are still in force today.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

The 13-month persistency rate is the standard industry metric for agent policy quality. It measures what percentage of the policies the agent wrote 13 months ago are still in force — i.e., still paying premiums and providing coverage. 13 months is chosen specifically because: the first grace period after the 12th month premium typically falls at month 13; and agent commission clawback provisions under most agreements cover the first 12 months. A persistency rate of 72% means that 72% of policies written 13 months ago are still active — 28% have lapsed.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Describes the agent's new business submission volume — a productivity metric, not a quality or persistency metric.
(B) Commission earned as a percentage of target is a financial performance measure — unrelated to the persistency calculation.
(D) Policy submission rate vs appointment rate is a conversion metric — measuring selling effectiveness, not the longevity of already-issued policies.

questions.stem: A Retirement Specialist in an annuity sales team is primarily responsible for:

opts.x: Processing group life scheme claims and managing employer relationships.
Advising retirees on annuity options, conducting retirement income planning, and managing the RSA fund transfer from the PFA to the insurer.
Training bank staff in bancassurance product knowledge and compliance.
Managing the insurer's relationships with telco and fintech distribution partners.

questions.answer: (B) Advising retirees on annuity options, conducting retirement income planning, and managing the RSA fund transfer from the PFA to the insurer.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

The Retirement Specialist role sits within the insurer's corporate and institutional sales team, specifically responsible for the Retirement Life Annuity product. Their work involves: engaging CPS retirees at the point of retirement; conducting retirement income planning (calculating the optimal lump sum vs annuity split); comparing annuity options (level vs escalating; single vs joint life; with vs without guarantee); processing the PenCom-mandated RSA fund transfer from the PFA to the life insurer; and ensuring all regulatory documentation is complete.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Group life claims management and employer relationship management are the Employee Benefit Consultant's responsibilities — a different role.
(C) Training bank staff in bancassurance is the Bancassurance Trainer's function — part of the bancassurance team, not the retirement specialist role.
(D) Telco and fintech distribution partner management falls to the Partnership Distribution team within the digital/Insurtech distribution function.

questions.stem: In a bancassurance partnership, the product shelf is best described as:

opts.x: The physical display rack of insurance brochures at the bank teller's counter.
The curated range of insurance products approved for distribution through the bancassurance channel, designed for simplicity and alignment with the bank's customer interaction moments.
The maximum commission rates the insurer is permitted to pay the bank under NAICOM guidelines.
The bank's own range of banking products that complement the insurer's life insurance offering.

questions.answer: (B) The curated range of insurance products approved for distribution through the bancassurance channel, designed for simplicity and alignment with the bank's customer interaction moments.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

The product shelf is a carefully curated selection of insurance products specifically designed or adapted for the bancassurance distribution environment. Key design principles: simplicity (bank staff are not specialist insurance advisers); alignment with natural customer interaction moments (salary account opening → term life; mortgage origination → credit life; fixed deposit maturity → annuity quotation referral); appropriate benefit levels for the bank's customer demographic; and regulatory compliance with the CBN-NAICOM Joint Guidelines.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Physical brochure displays are a marketing tactic, not the definition of the product shelf.
(C) Commission caps are a regulatory pricing matter — the product shelf is about product selection and design, not remuneration.
(D) The bank's own product range is separate from the insurance product shelf, though good bancassurance design creates integration points between them.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes an agritech platform distribution partnership for life insurance?

opts.x: A bank distributing life insurance to its agribusiness loan customers.
An insurer selling policies directly to agricultural workers through its own rural branch network.
A partnership in which an agritech company acts as a distribution partner, enabling the insurer to reach smallholder farmers through the agritech's existing platform and farmer relationships.
A joint venture between a life insurer and a state government to provide compulsory insurance for all registered farmers.

questions.answer: (C) A partnership in which an agritech company acts as a distribution partner, enabling the insurer to reach smallholder farmers through the agritech's existing platform and farmer relationships.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

Agritech distribution partnerships represent one of the most promising innovations in Nigerian financial inclusion for life insurance. Agritech platforms (companies providing farm management, input financing, or market access to smallholder farmers through mobile technology) have established trusted relationships with rural farmers — a segment that conventional insurance distribution has never reached effectively. By partnering with an agritech company, the life insurer accesses the agritech's farmer base through a trusted intermediary, using the agritech's mobile platform for policy issuance and premium collection.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) describes bancassurance targeting agribusiness clients — a different, bank-led model.
(B) A direct rural branch network would be prohibitively expensive to build and would not reach smallholder farmers at scale.
(D) A government compulsory scheme is a regulatory mandate — different from a commercial agritech distribution partnership.

questions.stem:
A life insurer’s retail agency branch has the following monthly performance data: 45 active agents; total AFYP submitted: ₦72 million; 13-month persistency rate: 54%; 8 agents (18%) submitted zero cases; average case size: ₦320,000. The target for the branch is: ₦90 million AFYP; 70% 13-month persistency; maximum 10% zero-case agents; average case size ₦450,000.
(a) Assess the branch’s performance against each target, identifying the most critical management priority.
(b) Describe three specific management interventions the branch manager should implement to address the persistency shortfall.
(c) Explain how the incentive structure described in this chapter (persistency bonus, qualification bonus, production club quality gate) would help address the identified performance gaps.
(d) What additional information would you want to analyse before deciding whether the zero-case agent issue reflects recruitment quality or management failure?

model.h: Part (a) — Performance Assessment and Critical Priority

rows: ₦72m vs ₦90m target — 80% achievement. Gap of ₦18m. Serious but recoverable.

54% vs 70% target — 16 percentage points below target. CRITICAL. This is the most important gap because it signals systematic product suitability failures, meaning revenue and profitability are being eroded at the base.
18% (8 agents) vs 10% target maximum — 8 percentage points worse. Significant but secondary.
₦320k vs ₦450k target — 71% achievement. Indicates agents are selling smaller, simpler products — may be linked to persistency issues if agents are targeting lower-income customers.

model.h: Most critical management priority: The 13-month persistency rate of 54% is the urgent priority. A 54% persistency rate means 46% of policies written 13 months ago have already lapsed — almost half. This level of lapse generates commission clawbacks, erodes the in-force renewal book, and signals systematic mis-selling. If this issue is not addressed, the branch's total in-force book is shrinking regardless of new business written.
Part (b) — Three Management Interventions for Persistency

1. Individual agent persistency review and coaching: The branch manager should pull the persistency data for each of the 45 agents individually. Persistency will not be uniformly distributed — 5–10 agents are likely responsible for the majority of lapses. For the worst-performing agents, conduct one-to-one coaching sessions reviewing: the customer profiles they are targeting; the product suitability conversations they are having; and whether their selling proposition is accurate. For agents with persistency below 40%, consider suspension from new business submission pending a remediation plan.

2. Customer contact programme for at-risk policies: Identify all policies in the branch's book that are in their 11th or 12th month of the first year — the highest lapse-risk window. Assign each at-risk policy to the original agent (or an orphan care agent if the original agent has left) for a proactive contact: confirm the premium due date, confirm the customer's continued satisfaction with the policy, offer a face-to-face review if the customer has questions. This direct conservation effort can improve 13-month persistency by 5–8 points within one renewal cycle.

3. Suitability documentation audit: Require all agents to complete and file a standardised suitability assessment form for every new policy going forward. The branch manager reviews a random 20% sample monthly. Any sale without documented suitability evidence is flagged. This creates compliance accountability and forces agents to have the affordability conversation before closing the sale.
Part (c) — How Incentive Structure Addresses Gaps

Persistency bonus: A quarterly persistency bonus (e.g., an additional 5% of AFYP for agents who maintain 70%+ persistency) directly rewards agents for quality over volume. An agent who writes fewer, better-matched policies earns more than one who writes more but loses them quickly. This is the most direct incentive addressing the 54% persistency gap.

Qualification bonus: An agent who completes advanced CIIN qualifications beyond the Cert. COP (Certificate, Diploma) receives a qualification bonus and a higher agency contract grade with better commission rates. This incentivises professional development — better-qualified agents sell more appropriately and achieve better persistency.

Production Club quality gate: A Production Club (the insurer's high-performer recognition programme) should require minimum persistency (e.g., 70%) as a qualifying criterion alongside minimum AFYP. An agent who achieves ₦10m AFYP with 45% persistency is explicitly excluded from Production Club membership. This sends a powerful cultural message that volume without quality is not recognised or rewarded.
Part (d) — Additional Information Before Diagnosing Zero-Case Agent Issue

Before attributing the 18% zero-case agent problem to recruitment quality or management failure, the branch manager should analyse:

1. Tenure profile of the zero-case agents: Are they all new agents (tenure < 3 months) who are still completing orientation and training? Newly appointed agents typically have a 2–3 month ramp-up period before their first case. If the zero-case agents are all very new, the issue may be a recruitment pipeline management problem rather than individual agent failure.

2. Attendance and activity data: Are the zero-case agents showing up for branch meetings, attending training sessions, and logging client approaches in the CRM? An agent who is attending and attempting but not converting has a different problem from one who has been invisible since appointment.

3. Prior persistency and conversion history: If any of the zero-case agents were previously productive and have recently dropped to zero, this may indicate a personal problem (health, financial stress, family issue) requiring a welfare conversation rather than a performance management action.

4. Recruiting manager's cohort: Which recruiting manager or Unit Manager appointed the zero-case agents? If 7 of the 8 zero-case agents were recruited by the same Unit Manager, the problem is likely a recruitment quality issue in that unit — the Unit Manager is appointing agents who are not serious committed sellers.

questions.stem:
A Nigerian commercial bank with 180 branches wants to launch a bancassurance partnership with a life insurer. The bank has chosen a full Corporate Agent Distribution Model (not a referral-only model).
(a) Describe the key provisions that should be included in the Master Distribution Agreement, with specific reference to product shelf design, staff training, premium remittance, and compliance obligations.
(b) Design a product shelf of three products appropriate for this bank’s customer base, explaining the natural customer journey moment for each product.
(c) Describe the training programme required to qualify bank tellers and relationship managers for bancassurance selling.
(d) How should the insurer monitor the bancassurance channel’s compliance with NIIRA 2025 market conduct obligations on an ongoing basis?

model.h: Part (a) — Master Distribution Agreement Key Provisions

1. Product shelf definition: The agreement specifies exactly which insurance products may be sold through the bancassurance channel, including: product names; sum assured ranges; premium levels; applicable customer eligibility criteria; and any product-specific selling restrictions (e.g., endowments only via Relationship Managers, not tellers).

2. Staff training and qualification: The bank commits to: ensuring all designated bancassurance staff hold the CIIN Cert. COP before selling; completing the insurer's product training for each product before it is offered; providing annual refresher training; and notifying the insurer within 5 days when a trained staff member leaves the bancassurance function.

3. Premium remittance: All premiums collected must be deposited into a segregated Premium Trust Account within 24 hours of collection; remittance to the insurer within 5 business days; monthly reconciliation statement provided to the insurer by the 5th of the following month; right of audit by the insurer over the trust account with 3 business days' notice.

4. Compliance obligations: The bank agrees to: maintain NAICOM corporate agent licence currency; comply with CBN-NAICOM Joint Guidelines; submit to quarterly compliance audits by the insurer; report all customer complaints relating to insurance products to the insurer within 3 days; and not engage in any prohibited practices (product bundling, pressure selling, misrepresentation of benefits).
Part (b) — Product Shelf Design for 180-Branch Commercial Bank

rows: Natural Customer Journey Moment and Design Rationale

Triggered at loan origination — the banker processes the loan application and the credit life policy is automatically included for loans above ₦10m (NIIRA 2025 mandatory). For smaller loans, it is offered as an optional product at an accessible premium. Simple declining benefit matching loan balance. No medical evidence required below the NML. Highest natural conversion moment in the entire bancassurance product shelf.

Triggered when a customer opens a new salary account or upgrades to a premium account tier. A straightforward 5-year term assurance (sum assured = 5–10× monthly salary; premium = 1–2% of sum assured per annum). Priced as a daily-expense-equivalent ('less than the cost of one lunch per week'). Tellers can complete the enrolment in the account opening workflow. No medical evidence required at standard sums assured.

Triggered when a customer with a child savings account, a school fees loan, or a child-tagged fixed deposit is identified. The teller or relationship manager introduces the concept and books a specialist life insurance adviser visit. The education endowment requires a more detailed suitability conversation — 15–20 year term, larger premiums, benefit illustration review. Not a teller-counter product but a Relationship Manager referral.

model.h: Part (c) — Training Programme

Phase 1 — Qualification (pre-deployment, 4–6 weeks):
• CIIN Cert. COP programme: The insurer partners with a CIIN-accredited training centre to deliver a compressed Cert. COP course for all designated bancassurance staff. Examinations sat and passed before any selling activity commences.

Phase 2 — Product Training (1 week per product):
• Credit life module: Product structure, mandatory NIIRA 2025 basis, application process, disclosure obligations, claim notification.
• Term assurance module: Product features, benefit illustration presentation, suitability criteria, common customer objections and accurate responses.
• Education endowment module (Relationship Managers only): How to identify and approach education planning conversations; referral to specialist protocol.

Phase 3 — Joint fieldwork (Week 1 of deployment):
• Trained bank staff shadow an experienced insurer representative for 3 days; then reverse — the insurer representative observes and coaches the bank staff in live customer interactions.

Phase 4 — Ongoing training:
• Monthly product knowledge refresh (30-minute session at branch level).
• Annual full product reaccreditation.
• Regulatory update briefings whenever NAICOM or CBN-NAICOM guidelines change.
Part (d) — Ongoing Market Conduct Monitoring

1. Mystery shopping programme: The insurer deploys trained mystery shoppers to selected bank branches quarterly, posing as customers at the point of sale. They assess: accuracy of product presentation; whether benefit illustrations were provided; whether suitability questions were asked; whether the cooling-off right was disclosed. Mystery shopping results are shared with the bank's bancassurance manager within 14 days.

2. Complaint analysis: All customer complaints relating to insurance products sold through the bancassurance channel are analysed monthly by the insurer's Market Conduct team. Patterns (e.g., repeated complaints about a specific branch or a specific product misrepresentation) trigger targeted investigation and remedial training.

3. Lapse rate monitoring by channel: The insurer tracks the 13-month persistency rate for policies sold through the bancassurance channel separately from the agency channel. Persistency below the agreed threshold in the Master Distribution Agreement triggers a compliance review of selling practices at the identified branches.

4. Annual market conduct audit: An annual formal audit of the bancassurance channel — reviewing a sample of customer files, suitability documentation, premium trust account records, and complaint handling — is conducted by the insurer's internal audit or compliance team. Findings are reported to the senior management of both the bank and the insurer.

questions.stem:
An Employee Benefit Consultant at a Nigerian life insurer has been asked to pitch for the group life business of a manufacturing company with 1,200 employees across four states. The company currently has no group life insurance despite the mandatory employer obligation. The company’s HR director has indicated that cost is the primary consideration.
(a) Describe the six stages of the corporate sales process for this opportunity and explain what information the EBC must gather at each stage.
(b) Explain the cross-selling opportunity between this group life scheme and the employees’ pension scheme, and how the EBC should position it.
(c) The HR director mentions that the CEO has died unexpectedly and the company is concerned about business continuity — identify the additional product opportunity this creates and how the EBC should respond.
(d) Describe the key performance indicators by which the EBC’s performance on this account should be measured after scheme implementation.

model.h: Part (a) — Six Stages of the Corporate Sales Process

Stage 1 — Prospecting and qualification: The EBC confirms the company's size (1,200 employees), states (four), industry (manufacturing), and current compliance status (no group life). Gathers initial information on the company's financial health (ability to pay premiums) and the HR director's decision-making authority. At this stage: gather employee headcount by grade, ATE range, and state-wise breakdown.

Stage 2 — Needs analysis: A structured fact-finding meeting with HR and CFO. Gather: full payroll data (ATE by employee to calculate minimum sum assured requirements); existing employee benefits (medical, pension); competitor benchmarking (what benefit levels do comparable manufacturers offer?); the company's compliance exposure under PRA 2014 and NIIRA 2025 (which the EBC uses to frame urgency).

Stage 3 — Design and quotation: The EBC designs the scheme structure: benefit multiple (3× ATE minimum; recommend 4× to be competitive); group rate based on payroll data and proposed FCL; premium calculations; optional add-ons (critical illness, accidental death benefit). Produce a formal quotation document.

Stage 4 — Presentation and handling objections: Present the quotation to the HR director (and ideally the CEO). The HR director's cost focus should be addressed by: (a) contextualising the PRA 2014 criminal liability for non-compliance — the legal risk is more expensive than the premium; (b) demonstrating that the group rate (₦0.15–₦0.20 per ₦1,000 SA) is modest relative to the risk managed.

Stage 5 — Negotiation and closing: Agree the benefit structure, premium, payment schedule, and scheme commencement date. Execute the master policy. Collect the first annual premium before commencement (no-premium-no-cover).

Stage 6 — Implementation and onboarding: Deliver employee data to the insurer; issue the master policy and employee membership certificates; conduct an employee communication session (in all four states); establish the claims contact protocol.
Part (b) — Cross-Selling Opportunity with Pension Scheme

The same 1,200-employee company is subject to PRA 2014 CPS contributions (assuming they have a registered PFA). The EBC should position the group life scheme as the protection layer complementing the pension accumulation:
• Group life (death in service benefit): Pays 3–4× ATE immediately on death — a lump sum available to the family within 30 days (no court order required under PRA 2014 Section 8(1)).
• CPS RSA balance: Accumulated pension savings passed to the estate, separately from the group life benefit.

The EBC should also investigate whether the company would benefit from:
1. An executive income protection product for senior management — covering salary continuation on long-term disability (a gap not addressed by group life).
2. A voluntary group savings plan — additional savings products for employees who want to supplement their CPS contributions.

The cross-sell conversation positions the EBC as a comprehensive employee benefits adviser rather than a single-product salesperson — building a deeper, longer-term relationship.
Part (c) — CEO Death: Keyman Insurance Opportunity

The CEO's unexpected death has created an acute and visceral demonstration to the company's board of the financial risk of key person dependency. The EBC should respond within days of learning this news:

'I was very sorry to hear about your CEO's passing. This is precisely the kind of event that keyman insurance is designed to address. May I ask — does the company have any keyman cover in place for the other members of your senior leadership team?'

The conversation should cover: identifying the 3–5 most financially critical individuals (Managing Director, Finance Director, key relationship holders); quantifying the financial loss the company would suffer from each person's death or disability (revenue impact, replacement cost, loan covenant triggers); designing keyman policies that would fund business continuity through the transition; and potentially also partnership insurance if shareholders need a buy-sell agreement.

The EBC should also present executive term assurance as a retention tool — offering senior managers life cover as a taxable benefit in kind, which is a valued component of an executive benefits package.
Part (d) — KPIs for EBC Performance After Implementation

rows: 100% — the scheme premium must be collected before each annual renewal. Any lapse is a critical failure for which the EBC is accountable.
+10% per annum minimum — through recruitment of new employees, salary increases (which raise ATE and therefore sum assured), and addition of optional add-on covers.
At least one additional product placed with the client within 12 months of group life inception (executive protection, voluntary savings plan, keyman).
Client-reported satisfaction score of 4.0/5 or above on the annual account review. Claims handling quality is the EBC's key deliverable.
100% — the employer must not switch insurer for purely cost reasons within 3 years. Persistency reflects the EBC's relationship quality and the scheme's service delivery.

questions.stem: The pyramid retail agency model has served as the backbone of individual life insurance distribution in Nigeria for decades, but it carries structural costs — high override expenses, agent attrition, persistency risk from commission-driven selling, and compliance exposure from the large untrained base — that may be incompatible with the NIIRA 2025 era’s regulatory and market demands. Critically evaluate whether the pyramid retail agency model remains fit for purpose as the primary distribution channel for individual life insurance in Nigeria, or whether a fundamental redesign — flat structures, salaried salesforces, digital-first models, or hybrid arrangements — is required. In your answer, address the economics of each model, the impact on product quality and persistency, the regulatory compliance requirements, and the market reach implications for Nigeria’s financial inclusion goals.

model.h: Thesis

The pyramid retail agency model is not inherently unfit for purpose — it is unfit for purpose as currently implemented and governed in the Nigerian market. Its economic structure can be preserved while its conduct pathologies are addressed. The alternatives (salaried salesforce, digital-first, flat structures) each solve some of the pyramid's problems while creating others. The outcome of this debate will determine the shape of Nigerian insurance distribution for a generation.
Economics of Each Model

Pyramid agency model economics: All distribution cost is variable — commission is paid only on production. The insurer bears minimal fixed cost. Unit Managers and Branch Managers are self-funding through overriders from their teams. First-year commission rates of 30–40% make product expensive but enable the extensive field force required to reach a market with low insurance awareness. At scale, the pyramid generates significant premium income but also creates high management cost at each supervisory level.

Salaried salesforce economics: Fixed distribution cost regardless of production. Suitable for products with very high success rates (group life with a corporate mandate) but financially destructive for individual life where sales cycles are long and rejection rates high. A salaried agent who fails to sell for 6 months is still costing the insurer their monthly salary.

Digital-first economics: Extremely low marginal distribution cost per policy at scale. But requires significant upfront technology investment and ongoing customer acquisition marketing cost. High CAC in the early phases before organic growth and referral effects emerge. Not suitable for complex products requiring human interaction.

Hybrid arrangement economics: A combination of digitally-enabled agents (who use technology for administration and lead management while retaining the human relationship) may be the most commercially optimal model — preserving the variable cost advantage while reducing the administrative inefficiency of fully paper-based agency.
Impact on Product Quality and Persistency

The pyramid model's persistency problem is well-documented (54% 13-month persistency in the Q6 example is not unusual for the Nigerian market). The structural cause is the misalignment between agent incentives (maximise first-year commission) and insurer interests (maximise long-term policy retention).

Redesign impact:
• Flat structure with persistency-weighted commission: If renewal commission is a larger proportion of total agent income (e.g., 30% first-year, 15% renewal for years 2–5), agents have a sustained financial interest in maintaining customer relationships. This structurally improves persistency.
• Smaller, professionalised agency force: A 30% reduction in agency headcount (from 3,000 to 2,100) with a corresponding increase in average agent quality (all Cert. COP; all above a minimum productiviyy threshold) produces better per-policy persistency and lower total commission payout for equivalent or higher premium income.
NIIRA 2025 Regulatory Compliance Requirements

NIIRA 2025 makes the status quo unsustainable in three ways:
1. Mandatory Cert. COP: An agency force with a significant proportion of unqualified or under-qualified sellers cannot continue. The pyramid model's traditional approach of appointing large numbers of part-time agents with minimal qualification must give way to a smaller, fully-qualified force.
2. TCF suitability assessment: Every individual life sale must be supported by a documented suitability assessment. This creates administrative burden that casual, part-time agents cannot sustain — favouring a smaller, full-time, better-governed agency structure.
3. Agent licensing: All agents must be individually licensed by NAICOM. The cost and administration of licensing 3,000+ agents and maintaining their compliance records is significant — pushing insurers toward smaller, higher-quality agency forces.
Market Reach and Financial Inclusion

Here is where the pyramid model's defenders make their strongest case: the pyramid's scale (3,000 agents in multiple states) creates distribution reach that no other model can replicate at comparable cost. If the insurer reduces from 3,000 to 1,000 agents, it loses presence in tier-2 and tier-3 cities — precisely the segments where financial inclusion is most needed and most underpenetrated.

The resolution: a two-tier distribution architecture. Tier 1 — a smaller (800–1,200 agent) fully qualified, highly productive retail agency force serving tier-1 cities and complex products. Tier 2 — digital and embedded distribution (USSD, MFB partnerships, agritech platforms) serving the mass market at scale with simple products. The pyramid does not disappear — it shrinks, professionalises, and is complemented by channels it cannot and should not compete with.

questions.stem: ‘The Nigerian life insurance company that will define the market’s next decade is not the one with the most agents or the biggest bank distribution partner — it is the one that builds the most intelligent multi-channel distribution ecosystem, with each channel designed for a specific customer segment, product type, and interaction model, and all channels managed with the discipline of precision measurement, active compliance oversight, and continuous digital integration.’ Critically evaluate this proposition. In your answer, assess the evidence for and against multi-channel distribution as the optimal strategy for a mid-size Nigerian life insurer; analyse the organisational and governance requirements of managing five or more active distribution channels simultaneously; evaluate the role of digital tools (CRM, agent app, analytics, virtual training) in making multi-channel management feasible at the insurer’s scale; and identify the two or three most critical management capabilities that separate a high-performing multi-channel distribution operation from one that achieves volume at the cost of compliance, quality, and policyholder trust.

model.h: Thesis

The proposition is directionally correct: the insurers that will dominate Nigerian life insurance in 2035 will be those with effective multi-channel architectures. But the proposition romanticises 'intelligence' — multi-channel distribution is genuinely difficult to manage well, and a poorly governed multi-channel operation is worse than a focused single-channel one. The competitive advantage lies not in the number of channels but in the discipline with which each is managed.
Evidence For Multi-Channel Strategy

1. Market segmentation reality: No single channel can serve all Nigerian consumer segments efficiently. The retail agency force reaches the aspiring middle class in Lagos and Abuja. Bancassurance reaches the bank's salary account holders. USSD reaches the unbanked informal sector. Agritech platforms reach smallholder farmers. Without all of these, the insurer is invisible to large portions of the addressable market.

2. Risk diversification: Dependence on a single distribution channel creates catastrophic revenue risk. An insurer dependent on a single bank partner for 70% of premium income is hostage to that bank's strategic priorities. Multi-channel distribution distributes this dependency.

3. Customer lifetime value: Research in other markets shows that customers acquired through multiple touchpoints (agent + digital + employer) have higher lifetime value — they are more likely to hold multiple products and less likely to lapse.
Evidence Against — Multi-Channel Complexity

1. Management attention and cost: Each channel requires dedicated management, training infrastructure, compliance oversight, technology integration, and performance management. A mid-size insurer with limited management depth may be unable to run five channels well simultaneously.

2. Brand consistency risk: Customers experience the insurer differently across channels — the agent is warm and personal; the USSD is transactional; the bancassurance interaction is bank-branded. Inconsistent customer experience across channels undermines brand coherence.

3. Channel conflict: Different channels serving overlapping segments create conflict (an agent calling on the same corporate client the bancassurance team has already approached; a digital lead being contacted by both an agent and a digital salesperson). Unmanaged channel conflict destroys customer experience and internal relationships.
Organisational and Governance Requirements for Five or More Channels

1. Dedicated channel leadership: Each major channel (retail agency, bancassurance, digital/embedded, corporate/EBC, microinsurance) requires a dedicated Channel Head with P&L accountability. Without clear ownership, channel management is diffuse and underperforms.

2. Central distribution governance: A Chief Distribution Officer (or equivalent) sits above all channel heads, managing channel conflict, optimising the customer segment-to-channel matching, and ensuring consistent brand standards across all channels.

3. Unified CRM: A single customer data platform that aggregates all customer interactions across all channels — so that if an agency client is also a bank customer, the insurer's systems recognise this and manage the relationship holistically. Without this, channels cannibalise each other and the customer experience is fragmented.

4. Channel-specific compliance oversight: Each channel has different market conduct risks (bancassurance has pressure-selling risk; digital has data privacy risk; agency has mis-selling risk). The compliance function must have channel-specific monitoring programmes, not a generic approach.
Digital Tools Enabling Multi-Channel Management

1. Agent mobile app: Reduces agent administrative burden (e-proposals, e-policy delivery, digital premium collection reminders), enables real-time performance tracking, and provides a compliance audit trail for suitability assessments across the agency network.

2. CRM with multi-channel customer view: Salesforce, HubSpot, or an equivalent platform that captures every customer interaction regardless of channel — enabling the insurer to see that a customer acquired digitally, serviced by an agent, and claims-supported through the contact centre is one person with a coherent relationship, not three separate data points.

3. Analytics for channel optimisation: Real-time dashboards tracking conversion rates, CAC, persistency, and complaint volumes by channel enable the distribution team to identify underperforming channels and reallocate resources dynamically.

4. Virtual training platforms: Enable continuous product and compliance training across all channels without the cost of assembling staff physically — particularly valuable for the distributed nature of agency and bancassurance networks.
Three Most Critical Management Capabilities

1. Segment-to-channel matching discipline: The ability to define precisely which customer segments each channel serves and to enforce those boundaries — preventing channel overlap, conflict, and customer confusion. This requires product design that differentiates by channel, not just by product feature.

2. Performance measurement precision: The capability to measure each channel's true profitability — not just AFYP, but contribution margin after CAC, commission, expected claims, and anticipated lapse. An insurer that cannot measure channel profitability accurately will systematically over-invest in the highest-volume but least-profitable channel.

3. Compliance oversight at channel level: The ability to monitor market conduct in each channel in real time — not through quarterly audits but through embedded data collection (complaint tagging, lapse attribution, mystery shopping) that provides continuous compliance signal. An insurer that discovers a channel compliance problem only at the annual audit has already damaged customer relationships, regulatory standing, and brand equity.
